Most of the time, when a student tells me they are bad at physics, what they
actually mean is that nobody has ever explained it to them in a language they
already speak. That is a translation problem, not an ability problem, and it is
fixable.

So this section exists to be the explanation I wish someone had handed me:
slower where it matters, honest about what is genuinely hard, and never
pretending a step is obvious when it isn't.

## How these are written

I try to hold to a few rules across everything in this section.

**Start below the starting point.** If a lesson needs an idea from three
courses ago, the lesson explains that idea rather than assuming it. The
Python series opens with information theory for exactly this reason.

**Name the hard part out loud.** Some things are genuinely difficult. Saying
"as you can clearly see" about a step that took me an hour is a disservice, and
it teaches students that their confusion is a personal failing.

**Give you something to poke at.** Reading about a `for` loop does very little.
Running one, breaking it, and running it again does quite a lot. Code on this
site is live wherever it can be.

**Keep the physics attached to something real.** Every abstraction started as
someone trying to answer a concrete question. That question is usually the
best way in.

There is more on where this comes from in my
[teaching philosophy](philosophy.qmd).
